title: A hard week at the care desk

review.notes: Built on the course: RATER, HEARD, de-escalation, recovery, chat tone, positive language, CSAT/NPS/FCR/service level/AHT formulas, CLV. All calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Northgate Home Appliances (fictional), a retailer with a call centre, WhatsApp care and 4 stores
content.briefing: You lead a care team of 12. A delivery partner failed this week, complaints are up, and the director wants a service scorecard on Friday. Handle the customers, coach your team and read the numbers.

variants.text: A customer shouts at the counter: his fridge delivery was missed twice and he took two days off work. Other customers are watching.

choices.t: Stay calm, use his name, agree with the facts, invite him to a quiet office
choices.f: His voice drops once he sits down. An audience keeps anger high; moving him helps you listen.

choices.t: Tell him firmly to calm down first, so that you can help him properly
choices.f: 'Calm down' makes it worse. He gets louder and posts about it online.

choices.t: Ask him to wait at the counter while you go and find the delivery manager
choices.f: Escalation may be needed later, but leaving him angry in front of others first loses control.

variants.text: A customer on the phone has explained her broken washing machine for three minutes. She is still talking. What do you do?

choices.t: Let her finish, then paraphrase and confirm the key facts
choices.f: She says 'yes, exactly'. Hear the full story first: anger falls when people feel heard.

choices.t: Interrupt politely to get her order number and save time
choices.f: You need the number, but interrupting early makes her repeat her story and feel rushed.

choices.t: Put her on hold while you check the order in the system
choices.f: Holding without explaining, mid-story, feels like being ignored. She asks for a manager.

variants.text: Using HEARD, you have heard the story and shown empathy. The delivery partner was at fault. What comes next?

choices.t: Apologise sincerely, then fix it: a confirmed delivery slot
choices.f: Correct order: Apologise, Resolve, then Diagnose the cause. He accepts a slot with a two-hour window.

choices.t: Explain that the delivery partner caused it, not the store
choices.f: Blame shifting. To the customer, the partner is your company.

choices.t: Diagnose the root cause with the partner before promising anything
choices.f: Diagnosis matters, but it comes last. The customer needs a resolution now.

variants.text: The missed delivery cost a customer two days off work. The fridge now arrives tomorrow. What else do you do?

choices.t: Add a fair gesture, such as free delivery, and call after delivery
choices.f: Good recovery: fix fast, a fair gesture for a real loss, and a follow-up. She later rates the service 5.

choices.t: Nothing more; the fridge is now arriving
choices.f: The problem is solved, but the loss is ignored. She stays, but she tells friends about the wait.

choices.t: Offer a 50% refund on the fridge to end the complaint
choices.f: Far beyond the loss. Gestures should be fair, and this sets an expensive example.

variants.text: A WhatsApp reply drafted by a new agent: 'ORDER DELAYED!!! WE DON'T KNOW WHEN. PROBLEM WITH DELIVERY.' How do you rewrite it?

choices.t: Greet, name, short apology, what you are doing, reply time 14:00
choices.f: No capitals, one topic per message, and a time instead of 'soon'. The customer thanks you.

choices.t: Keep the facts, remove the capitals and exclamation marks
choices.f: Better tone, but it still says what you cannot do and gives no time.

choices.t: Send it as is; customers want honesty and speed
choices.f: Capitals read as shouting, and 'we don't know' with no next step makes the customer escalate.

variants.text: A customer asks if the oven can be installed today. Installers are booked until Thursday. What do you say?

choices.t: 'I can book an installer for Thursday at 9:00. Shall I confirm it?'
choices.f: Say what you can do and give a time. She books Thursday.

choices.t: 'No, that is not possible today. Installers are fully booked.'
choices.f: Says only what you cannot do. She hangs up to call a competitor.

choices.t: 'Unfortunately there is a problem with installer availability.'
choices.f: Polite, but 'problem' with no next step leaves her asking 'so when?'.

variants.text: A caller insults your agent with abusive language and refuses to stop after a polite warning.

choices.t: Set the boundary clearly, then end the call and log it
choices.f: Correct. Set limits politely for abuse; staff safety and dignity come first.

choices.t: Keep listening; the customer is always right
choices.f: No one should accept abuse. Your agent leaves the shift upset.

choices.t: Transfer the call to you so the agent is spared
choices.f: Kind to the agent, but the abuse continues. A clear boundary is still needed.

variants.text: A customer asks for a refund larger than your authority allows. He is calm but firm.

choices.t: Escalate to the person who can approve it, and tell him when he will hear
choices.f: Escalate when beyond your authority, and set expectations. He gets an answer the same day.

choices.t: Approve it yourself now so he does not have to wait any longer
choices.f: You exceed your authority. Finance reverses it and the customer is angrier.

choices.t: Tell him that refunds of that size are not possible in this store
choices.f: That is not true. It is only beyond your level. He complains to head office.

variants.text: NPS survey: 200 responses. 110 scored 9-10, 50 scored 7-8, 40 scored 0-6. What is the NPS?

choices.f: Correct: 55% promoters minus 20% detractors.
That is only the share of promoters. NPS subtracts the detractors.
You counted passives as promoters. Passives (7-8) are left out.

variants.text: CSAT survey: 300 responses, 240 rated 4 or 5. What is CSAT?

choices.f: Correct: 240 / 300 x 100.
CSAT is the percentage of 4 and 5 ratings, not an average score.
Wrong count. Use responses of 4 or 5 divided by all responses.

variants.text: Yesterday 1,000 calls were offered and 720 were answered within 20 seconds. The target is 80/20. What is the service level, and is it met?

choices.t: 72%: below target
choices.f: Correct: 720 / 1,000 x 100. You check staffing at the peak hours.

choices.t: 72%: on target
choices.f: The target is 80% within 20 seconds. 72% misses it.

choices.t: 28%: below target
choices.f: That is the share answered late. Service level = answered within target / offered x 100.

variants.text: This month, 800 issues were raised and 600 were solved at the first contact. What is FCR?

choices.f: Correct: 600 / 800 x 100. FCR saves cost and customer effort.
That is the share needing repeat contact.
You divided the wrong way round. FCR = solved first time / total issues.

variants.text: The director wants to cut average handling time from 7.5 to 5 minutes and rank agents on it.

choices.t: Balance AHT with FCR and CSAT so speed does not cut quality
choices.f: Correct. AHT alone pushes agents to rush and customers call back. Speed is not service.

choices.t: Agree; faster calls mean more calls answered
choices.f: Agents rush, FCR falls and repeat calls rise. Total workload goes up.

choices.t: Refuse to measure AHT at all
choices.f: AHT is useful for staffing. The issue is using it as the only target.

variants.text: An agent's call: talk 300 seconds, hold 60 seconds, after-call work 90 seconds. What is the handling time for this call?

choices.t: 450 seconds (7.5 minutes)
choices.f: Correct: talk + hold + after-call work.

choices.t: 300 seconds (5 minutes)
choices.f: You counted talk time only. Hold and after-call work are part of handling.

choices.t: 360 seconds (6 minutes)
choices.f: After-call work is missing. AHT includes it.

variants.text: A loyal customer spends Kz 20,000 a visit, 12 visits a year, for about 5 years, at a 25% margin. What is the lifetime profit at risk if she leaves?

choices.f: Correct: 20,000 x 12 x 5 = 1,200,000 revenue x 25% margin.
That is lifetime revenue. Multiply by margin to get profit.
That is one year's profit. Lifetime value counts all the years.

variants.text: Agents say the stock system is slow and the refund policy keeps changing. Service quality is falling.

choices.t: Fix internal service first: tools and clear policy for agents
choices.f: The service-profit chain: internal service quality drives staff satisfaction and then customer value.

choices.t: Run a smile-and-courtesy training for all agents
choices.f: Courtesy helps, but agents with bad tools still fail customers.

choices.t: Add a target for complaints closed per agent
choices.f: Pressure without tools means agents close complaints without solving them.

variants.text: You write a new service standard for WhatsApp. Which one is a real standard?

choices.t: 'We reply to every WhatsApp within 15 minutes, 8:00 to 20:00'
choices.f: Correct: measurable, specific, observable and timed.

choices.t: 'We always reply to customers as fast as possible'
choices.f: Not measurable. Nobody can check 'as fast as possible'.

choices.t: 'We give friendly, excellent service on every channel'
choices.f: A slogan, not a standard. It has no target or time.

variants.text: A customer's broken-oven case is beyond the front line. Specialists in Tier 2 handle repairs. What kind of escalation is this?

choices.t: Functional escalation to more skill
choices.f: Correct. Hierarchical escalation is to more authority, such as a manager.

choices.t: Hierarchical escalation to more authority
choices.f: That is for decisions beyond your authority. Here you need technical skill.

choices.t: No escalation; the agent should keep trying
choices.f: Keeping a case at the front line beyond its skill wastes the customer's time.

variants.text: The scorecard shows CSAT is up 3 points, but comments mention long waits for callbacks.

choices.t: Read the comments, act on the callbacks, and report both
choices.f: Scores show what; comments show why. The director agrees to fix the callback queue.

choices.t: Report the CSAT rise; comments are only a few opinions
choices.f: Ignoring comments hides the next problem. What gets measured gets managed only if you read it.

choices.t: Wait for next month to see if comments repeat
choices.f: Watching trends is fine, but a clear signal deserves action now.

variants.text: A customer's issue needs checking with the warehouse. You will know in about two hours.

choices.t: 'I will check with the warehouse and reply by 14:00 today.'
choices.f: Set expectations with a time. You reply at 13:40 and the customer is pleased.

choices.t: 'I will get back to you as soon as possible.'
choices.f: Polite, but 'as soon as possible' means different things. He calls back twice.

choices.t: 'Please call us again later today for an update.'
choices.f: You push the effort onto the customer. High effort predicts customers leaving.
